distractorStrategy: The printed value assumed to be returned — the single most valuable distractor in this skill. Also the last assignment inside the body assumed to be returned, and an error claimed at the point of definition.
notes: The print/return confusion is the defining Foundation error with functions.

factStatement: Each call starts fresh; values from a previous call do not carry over.
familyName: Reasoning about repeated calls
measurementObjective: Give the results of two successive calls to the same function.
distractorStrategy: The second call assumed to continue from the first, so a local counter appears to accumulate; both calls assumed to return the first result; an error claimed on the second call.

factStatement: A name created inside a function exists only while it runs and cannot be used outside.
familyName: What is visible outside a function
measurementObjective: Say whether a name is available after the function returns, and what happens if it is used.
distractorStrategy: The local assumed visible outside; the local assumed to overwrite an outer name of the same name; the value assumed to persist between calls.

factStatement: A parameter or local with the same name as an outer variable is a different variable; changing it leaves the outer one alone.
familyName: Reasoning about two variables with one name
measurementObjective: Give the value of the outer variable after a function that assigns to a same-named local.
distractorStrategy: The outer variable assumed changed — the whole point. Also an error claimed for reusing the name, and the two values assumed to be combined.

factStatement: A function with no return gives back nothing usable, even if it printed something.
familyName: Choosing between returning and printing
measurementObjective: Decide which of two functions can have its result used in a further calculation, and why.
distractorStrategy: The printing version claimed usable because the value was visible; both claimed equivalent; the returning version claimed to print. Show two functions differing only in return versus print.
notes: Same fact as FN_FAM07, at the level of choosing rather than predicting.

factStatement: A long piece of code can be split into functions that each do one nameable thing.
familyName: Choosing a useful split into functions
measurementObjective: Choose the split whose functions each do one thing and together cover the task.
distractorStrategy: A split that leaves part of the task in no function; one whose functions each need the others half-finished; one that splits on line count rather than on responsibility. All options must be syntactically fine, so the judgement is about structure.
notes: Ties back to PS_FAM06. Different skill, so a separate reassessment group by rule; noted here because the two measure related judgement.

factStatement: A function that returns the wrong thing usually has a misplaced return, a shadowed name, or nothing returned at all.
familyName: Diagnosing why a function gives the wrong result
measurementObjective: Given a function and a wrong result, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A return placed inside a loop so it exits on the first item; a printed value where a return was needed; an outer variable relied on instead of a parameter. Every option must be a real fault pattern, with only one producing the stated symptom.
notes: Return-inside-the-loop is the canonical D5 stem: the function works for single-item input and fails otherwise.

factStatement: A function correct for ordinary arguments can fail or return something wrong for empty, zero or boundary arguments.
familyName: Behaviour of a function on an extreme argument
measurementObjective: Say what a function returns for an empty, zero or boundary argument.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary-argument result; a failure where nothing is returned quietly; a returned value where it genuinely fails. Distinguishing "returns nothing" from "fails" is the measurement.

factStatement: A branch lets work proceed without affecting another line of development.
familyName: Recognising what a branch is for
measurementObjective: Identify what branching makes possible that working in one line does not.
distractorStrategy: A branch described as a copy of the folder; as a backup; as a way to give each person their own project. The copy belief blocks understanding of merging.

factStatement: A branch is a named position in the history, not a separate copy of the files.
familyName: Recognising what a branch actually is
measurementObjective: Say what exists when a branch is created and what does not.
distractorStrategy: Creating a branch assumed to duplicate every file; assumed to change the current files; assumed to require a remote. The duplication belief explains why students fear branching.

factStatement: Merging brings the commits of one branch into another, combining both sets of changes.
familyName: Recognising what merging achieves
measurementObjective: Identify what a merge produces and which branch it changes.
distractorStrategy: A merge assumed to change both branches; assumed to delete the source branch; assumed to keep only the newer file of each pair.

factStatement: A new commit is added to whichever branch is currently checked out.
familyName: Which branch a commit lands on
measurementObjective: Given a sequence of switches and commits, say which branch holds which commit.
distractorStrategy: Commits assumed to land on the main line regardless; assumed to appear on every branch; assumed to follow the branch they were begun on rather than the current one.
notes: Show the switch/commit sequence in the stem.

factStatement: Switching branches changes the files in the working folder to match that branch.
familyName: What switching changes on disk
measurementObjective: Say what the working folder contains after switching branches.
distractorStrategy: The files assumed unchanged by a switch; assumed to merge from both branches; work from one branch assumed to disappear permanently. Distinguish "not visible now" from "lost".

factStatement: A commit on one branch does not change any other branch until the two are merged.
familyName: Reasoning about what a branch does not see
measurementObjective: Say what one branch contains after work has been done on another.
distractorStrategy: Changes assumed to propagate automatically; the newer branch assumed to be authoritative; a file assumed shared because it has the same name.

factStatement: After a successful merge the target branch contains both sets of changes.
familyName: What each branch holds after a merge
measurementObjective: Given two branches and a merge, say what each contains afterwards.
distractorStrategy: Only the newer changes surviving; both branches assumed updated; the source branch assumed emptied. Two branches that changed different files is the clearest stem.

factStatement: Two branches share their history up to the point they diverged, and differ only after it.
familyName: Reading where two branches diverged
measurementObjective: Given a history diagram in the stem, say which commits are shared and which are unique.
distractorStrategy: All commits assumed shared; none assumed shared; the divergence point placed one commit out. The diagram must be readable and must decide the answer.
notes: Show the history as ASCII in the stem.

factStatement: A conflict arises when both branches changed the same part of the same file, not merely the same file.
familyName: Predicting whether a merge conflicts
measurementObjective: Given what each branch changed, say whether merging conflicts and why.
distractorStrategy: Any change to one file assumed to conflict — the belief that makes students avoid branching; different files assumed to conflict; identical changes assumed to conflict.
notes: Include a same-file, different-region case, which must NOT conflict.

factStatement: Resolving a conflict means deciding what the combined file should say; the tool cannot decide for you.
familyName: Reasoning about a resolved file
measurementObjective: Given a conflicted file shown in the stem, choose the correct resolved content.
distractorStrategy: A resolution leaving the conflict markers in place — the commonest real error; one keeping only one side when both changes were needed; one that is valid but discards a change silently.
notes: Show the markers verbatim.

factStatement: A merge creates a point where two lines of history join, and the shape records what happened.
familyName: Reading the shape of a merged history
measurementObjective: Given a history shape, say how many branches contributed and where they joined.
distractorStrategy: A linear reading of a merged history; the merge point read as the divergence point; a branch counted twice. Conceptual only — no rebase at Foundation.

factStatement: Work committed to the wrong branch is present but not where it is expected, and is still recoverable.
familyName: Diagnosing work on the wrong branch
measurementObjective: Given the symptom that a change is missing from one branch and present in another, identify what happened.
distractorStrategy: The work assumed lost; a remote problem blamed; the file assumed deleted. Distinguishing "on another branch" from "gone" is the measurement.

factStatement: A change that exists on a branch and not in the shared line has not been merged, whatever else was done.
familyName: Diagnosing an unmerged change
measurementObjective: Given several branches and a missing feature, identify which merge was never performed.
distractorStrategy: A merge that was performed; sending blamed for a merge omission; the feature assumed broken rather than absent. D5 uses three branches where two merges happened and one did not.

factStatement: The order in which branches are merged changes how much conflict resolution is needed and what the history shows.
familyName: Choosing an order to merge several branches
measurementObjective: Given three branches with overlapping changes, choose the merge order that resolves each conflict once.
distractorStrategy: An order requiring the same conflict to be resolved twice; one that loses a change; one that appears simplest but merges into the wrong target. All orders must be possible.

factStatement: How much work belongs on one branch is a judgement: too much makes merging hard, too little makes the history noise.
familyName: Judging what belongs on one branch
measurementObjective: Given a described piece of work, choose the branching approach and justify it.
distractorStrategy: One branch for everything; a branch per file; a branch per person regardless of the work. Each is a real habit with a real cost, and the cost must be what decides.
notes: Judgement, not house style. The stem must state what matters for this project.

factStatement: Version control keeps a history of recorded states, so an earlier version can be recovered.
familyName: Recognising what version control provides
measurementObjective: Identify what version control gives you that copying folders does not.
distractorStrategy: Version control described as a backup of the current state only; as a way to share files; as automatic saving of every keystroke. The last matters because students who believe it do not commit.

factStatement: A repository is a project folder together with the recorded history of its changes.
familyName: Recognising what a repository contains
measurementObjective: Say what is inside a repository and what is not.
distractorStrategy: A repository as a folder on a website; as only the latest files; as something that exists only once the project is shared. The third is why beginners think they need an account to start.

factStatement: Each everyday command moves work between the working folder, the staged set and the recorded history.
familyName: Matching a command to what it moves
measurementObjective: Given a command, say which transition it performs.
distractorStrategy: Staging confused with committing; committing believed to publish to the remote; a command that reads history offered as one that changes it. The commit-publishes belief is the most consequential.
notes: Named commands are unavoidable here, but the answer is always the transition, never the spelling.

factStatement: A change is modified, staged, or committed, and only a committed change is part of the history.
familyName: Telling a staged change from a recorded one
measurementObjective: Given a described sequence, say which state a file is in.
distractorStrategy: Staged treated as saved into history; a modified-but-unstaged file treated as included in the next commit; a committed file treated as still staged.
notes: The load-bearing concept of the whole skill.

factStatement: A commit records the staged changes with a message, and does not include work that was never staged.
familyName: What a commit does and does not contain
measurementObjective: Given files in mixed states, say which are captured by the next commit.
distractorStrategy: Every changed file assumed included; only the last edited file included; changes made after staging assumed to be captured. The third is subtle and common.
notes: Editing a file after staging it is the sharpest stem.

factStatement: A change is modified, staged, or committed, and only a committed change is part of the history.
familyName: Tracing file state through a sequence of commands
measurementObjective: Give the state of each named file after a short run of commands.
distractorStrategy: The state one command earlier; every file assumed to move together; a file assumed to leave the working folder once committed. Show the command sequence in the stem.
notes: Same fact as GF_FAM04, traced rather than defined.

factStatement: The local history and the remote history are separate and only match when changes are deliberately sent or fetched.
familyName: Reasoning about which history holds what
measurementObjective: Say which of the local and remote histories contains a described change.
distractorStrategy: A commit assumed to appear on the remote immediately; the remote assumed to be the only real history; a teammate assumed to see uncommitted work. This is the misconception behind most "my code is gone" reports.

factStatement: Sending publishes local commits; fetching brings remote commits down. Neither happens on its own.
familyName: What sending and fetching change
measurementObjective: Say what each side holds after a described send or fetch.
distractorStrategy: Sending assumed to also bring changes down; fetching assumed to overwrite local work; either assumed to include uncommitted changes.

factStatement: The history is an ordered record, most recent first, and each entry names what changed and when.
familyName: Answering a question from a history listing
measurementObjective: Given a history listing in the stem, answer which change came first or which commit introduced something.
distractorStrategy: The listing read bottom-up as chronological; the most recent entry assumed to contain every change; a message assumed to describe the whole state rather than one change.
notes: Show a real listing. The item is unanswerable without reading it, which is the point.

factStatement: An ignored file is left out of the history but still exists in the working folder.
familyName: What ignoring a file does
measurementObjective: Say what happens to an ignored file locally and in the history.
distractorStrategy: Ignoring assumed to delete the file; assumed to remove a file already committed (it does not); assumed to hide it from the working folder. The already-committed case is the D4 measurement.

factStatement: Work that has never been committed is not in the history and cannot be recovered from it.
familyName: Deciding what survives a mishap
measurementObjective: Given a described accident, say which work can still be recovered.
distractorStrategy: Uncommitted work assumed recoverable because the project is under version control; committed work assumed lost because the folder was damaged; staged-but-uncommitted work treated as safe.
notes: The single most valuable family for preventing real loss.

factStatement: Each everyday command moves work between the working folder, the staged set and the recorded history.
familyName: Choosing the command for a stated goal
measurementObjective: Given a goal, choose the command that achieves it without doing more than asked.
distractorStrategy: A command that achieves the goal and discards other work; one that only appears to (staging where committing was needed); one that acts on the remote where the goal was local.
notes: Same fact as GF_FAM03, choosing rather than recognising.

conceptName: Why is my change not there
factStatement: A change that is not where it is expected has stopped at a specific point: unsaved, unstaged, uncommitted or unsent.
familyName: Locating where a change stopped
measurementObjective: Given a symptom — a teammate cannot see the change, the history does not show it — identify which step was not done.
distractorStrategy: Steps that were done; a remote problem blamed for a local omission; the file blamed rather than the workflow. The symptom must implicate exactly one missing step.
notes: The most useful diagnostic family in the skill; D5 uses a symptom with two plausible causes distinguished by one detail.

factStatement: What can be recovered is exactly what was recorded, so the recovery options depend on what was committed and when.
familyName: Reasoning about recovery options
measurementObjective: Given a history and a mistake, decide what can be restored and from where.
distractorStrategy: Recovery of work never committed; a recovery that discards later legitimate commits; a recovery from the remote where the remote never received it. Every option must be a real operation.

factStatement: The order in which people record, fetch and send determines whether work is lost or preserved.
familyName: Choosing a safe order of operations
measurementObjective: Given two people working on the same project, choose the order of operations that loses nothing.
distractorStrategy: An order that overwrites the other person; one that works only if nobody else changed anything; one that avoids loss but discards the local work. All options must be sequences a beginner would plausibly try.

factStatement: Each element states what a piece of content IS, not how it looks.
familyName: Matching content to the element that describes it
measurementObjective: Given a piece of content, choose the element whose meaning fits it.
distractorStrategy: An element chosen for its default appearance rather than its meaning — a heading used to make text big, a list used for indentation, a quote used to indent. That confusion is the whole reason semantics is taught.

factStatement: An element is written as an opening tag, content, and a closing tag, and some elements have no content.
familyName: Recognising well-formed element syntax
measurementObjective: Identify which of several fragments is written correctly.
distractorStrategy: A missing closing tag; a closing tag for an element that takes none; tags closed in the wrong order. All must look plausible at a glance.
notes: Foundation-critical rather than trivia: malformed markup is where beginners lose an afternoon.

factStatement: An attribute supplies information about an element, written inside its opening tag.
familyName: Recognising an attribute and its role
measurementObjective: Given a tag, identify its attributes and what each supplies.
distractorStrategy: The element name read as an attribute; content read as an attribute value; an attribute placed in the closing tag.

factStatement: Elements nest inside one another and must be closed in the reverse order they were opened.
familyName: Judging whether nesting is valid
measurementObjective: Identify the fragment whose elements nest correctly.
distractorStrategy: Overlapping tags closed in the wrong order; a block element inside an inline one; an element nested where it is not permitted. Overlap is the one that renders unpredictably.

factStatement: Each element states what a piece of content IS, not how it looks.
familyName: Choosing between two elements that look the same
measurementObjective: Given two elements with similar default rendering, choose the one whose meaning is right.
distractorStrategy: The visually identical but semantically wrong element; a generic container where a specific element exists; an element chosen because it is shorter to type.
notes: Same fact as HT_FAM01, discriminating rather than recalling.

factStatement: The markup determines the structure the browser displays, including whitespace it collapses.
familyName: Predicting what markup displays
measurementObjective: Given a fragment, say what appears on the page.
distractorStrategy: Line breaks in the source assumed to appear on the page; repeated spaces assumed preserved; a tag assumed to be displayed as text. Whitespace collapsing is the productive case.
notes: Show markup with deliberate whitespace in the stem.

factStatement: Lists and tables have required inner elements, and content outside them is not part of the structure.
familyName: Building or reading a list or table structure
measurementObjective: Given a list or table fragment, say how many items or cells it produces.
distractorStrategy: Text placed directly inside a list counted as an item; a row counted as a cell; a header row omitted from the count. Row and cell counting is the sharpest form.

factStatement: A relative path is resolved from the location of the page containing it.
familyName: Working out where a link leads
measurementObjective: Given a folder layout and a link, say which file it reaches.
distractorStrategy: A relative path resolved from the site root; a parent step miscounted; a leading slash treated as relative. Show the folder tree in the stem so the answer is derivable.
notes: Overlaps OS_FAM07 on paths. Different skill, so a separate reassessment group by rule; noted because the reasoning is the same.

factStatement: A form control needs a name for its value to be submitted, and its type decides how it behaves.
familyName: Predicting what a form submits
measurementObjective: Given a form fragment, say which values are submitted.
distractorStrategy: A control with no name assumed to submit; a disabled control assumed to submit; an unchecked box assumed to submit a false value. The unnamed control is the classic silent failure.

factStatement: Alternative text describes an image for anyone who cannot see it, and an empty value means the image is decorative.
familyName: Choosing alternative text for an image
measurementObjective: Given an image and its role on the page, choose the appropriate alternative text.
distractorStrategy: The filename as the text; a description of appearance rather than meaning; text supplied for a purely decorative image. The decorative case, where empty is correct, is the D4 measurement.

factStatement: Nested markup forms a tree, in which elements have parents, children and siblings.
familyName: Reading parent, child and sibling relationships
measurementObjective: Given a fragment, identify an element's parent, children or siblings.
distractorStrategy: A grandparent named as the parent; a nephew named as a sibling; text content omitted from the children. Indentation in the stem must be exact.
notes: The bridge into CSS selectors and the DOM; worth measuring here rather than assuming it.

factStatement: A markup mistake produces a characteristic symptom on the page rather than an error message.
familyName: Locating the markup fault from the symptom
measurementObjective: Given a page that renders wrongly, identify the line at fault.
distractorStrategy: Lines that are correct; a fault that would give a different symptom; a styling cause where the fault is structural. The symptom must implicate one line.

factStatement: Correct structure and labelling are what make a page usable by assistive technology.
familyName: Judging whether markup is usable without sight
measurementObjective: Given a fragment, identify what a screen reader user would be unable to do and why.
distractorStrategy: A visual fix offered for a structural problem; a label present but not associated with its control; a heading level skipped. Every option must look fine on screen, which is the point.

factStatement: An unclosed element swallows the content after it, so the symptom appears far from the mistake.
familyName: Reasoning about a fault whose symptom is elsewhere
measurementObjective: Given a page where later content is misplaced, identify the earlier unclosed element.
distractorStrategy: The element where the symptom appears blamed rather than the one that caused it; a correctly closed element blamed; a CSS cause proposed. Distance between cause and symptom is the measurement.
notes: The most transferable debugging idea in the skill: the fault is upstream of the symptom.

factStatement: Two fragments can render identically while differing in meaning and accessibility.
familyName: Judging whether two fragments are truly equivalent
measurementObjective: Decide whether two fragments are equivalent in structure and meaning, not merely in appearance.
distractorStrategy: A pair identical on screen and different in meaning — the central case; a pair differing only in whitespace, which IS equivalent; a pair differing in nesting depth with no visible effect.
notes: Include at least one genuinely equivalent pair, or the family teaches that different markup always differs.

factStatement: A rule pairs a selector with declarations, each a property and a value.
familyName: Identifying the parts of a rule
measurementObjective: Given a rule, name its selector, properties and values.
distractorStrategy: The property named as the selector; the value named as the property; the whole declaration named as the selector.

factStatement: Each property changes one aspect of presentation.
familyName: Matching a property to its effect
measurementObjective: Given a desired visual change, choose the property that produces it.
distractorStrategy: Properties confused in pairs students genuinely mix up: margin against padding, colour against background colour. Not obscure properties, which measure vocabulary rather than understanding.

factStatement: A selector can target an element type, a class, or an identifier, and each is written differently.
familyName: Recognising what kind of selector this is
measurementObjective: Given a selector, say what it targets.
distractorStrategy: Class and identifier prefixes swapped; a descendant selector read as two separate selectors; an element selector read as a class.

factStatement: A selector matches every element satisfying it, which may be none, one or many.
familyName: Deciding which elements a selector matches
measurementObjective: Given markup and a selector, say how many elements it matches and which.
distractorStrategy: A descendant selector read as requiring a direct child; a class selector assumed to match one element only; nested matches missed. Show markup and selector together.

factStatement: Some properties pass down to descendants and others do not.
familyName: Deciding whether a style reaches a child
measurementObjective: Given a rule on a parent, say whether a child is affected.
distractorStrategy: Every property assumed to inherit; none assumed to; a border assumed inherited because colour is. The mixed case is the whole measurement.

factStatement: When two rules apply, the more specific one wins, and between equals the later one wins.
familyName: Deciding which of two rules applies
measurementObjective: Given competing rules, say which value the element ends up with.
distractorStrategy: The later rule assumed to win regardless of specificity; the first rule assumed to win; both assumed to apply and blend. Order and specificity must point different ways in at least one variant.
notes: The single most useful family in the skill: nearly every real CSS confusion is a cascade question.

factStatement: Selectors can be compared for specificity, with identifiers beating classes and classes beating element names.
familyName: Comparing two selectors for specificity
measurementObjective: Given two selectors, say which is more specific.
distractorStrategy: Length mistaken for specificity — a long element chain beaten by one class; the count of parts used instead of their kinds; inline style assumed to be a normal rule.
notes: Conceptual comparison, not numeric weight arithmetic.

factStatement: An element occupies its content plus padding, border and margin, and which of those count toward its stated width depends on the sizing rule.
familyName: Working out the space an element occupies
measurementObjective: Given content width, padding and border, give the total space occupied.
distractorStrategy: Padding omitted; border omitted; margin counted inside the element. Each is arithmetic that reveals a specific gap, and the numbers must be small enough that the item is not a calculation exercise.

factStatement: Whether an element takes a full line or sits inline is decided by its display behaviour, not by its content.
familyName: Predicting whether elements sit side by side
measurementObjective: Given markup and display values, say how the elements are arranged.
distractorStrategy: Inline elements assumed to accept a height; block elements assumed to sit side by side; width assumed to apply to an inline element. The last is the classic "why is my width ignored".

factStatement: Some units are fixed and others are relative to the parent or the viewport, so the same number means different sizes.
familyName: Reasoning about what a unit resolves to
measurementObjective: Given a value in a relative unit and its context, say what size results.
distractorStrategy: A percentage resolved against the viewport rather than the parent; a relative font unit resolved against the root when it inherits; a fixed unit assumed to scale.

factStatement: A layout is the combined effect of several rules, and the result can be predicted from them.
familyName: Predicting the arrangement several rules produce
measurementObjective: Given markup and a small stylesheet, choose the arrangement produced.
distractorStrategy: The arrangement one rule would give alone; the arrangement with the rules applied in the wrong order; a layout that would need a rule not present. Describe arrangements in words, since options cannot be images.
notes: Keep the stylesheet to three or four rules so the item stays a reasoning task.

factStatement: Styles can be made conditional on screen width, and apply only while the condition holds.
familyName: Deciding which styles apply at a given width
measurementObjective: Given conditional rules and a screen width, say which styles are in effect.
distractorStrategy: A boundary width assigned to the wrong side; conditional styles assumed to replace all others rather than adding to them; overlapping conditions assumed exclusive. Ask about the exact boundary width.

conceptName: Why is my style not applied
factStatement: A style that appears to do nothing has a specific cause: it did not match, it was overridden, or the property does not apply to that element.
familyName: Diagnosing a style that had no effect
measurementObjective: Given markup, a stylesheet and a style that is not visible, identify why.
distractorStrategy: A syntax cause where the rule is fine and simply lost the cascade; a specificity cause where the selector never matched; a caching cause where the rule was overridden. The three real causes must be separable from the evidence given.
notes: The most common real CSS question a student will ever ask, and the reason this family carries D5 weight.

factStatement: Overriding a style means winning the cascade, which can be done by specificity, by order, or by changing the selector.
familyName: Choosing how to override an existing style
measurementObjective: Given a style you cannot edit, choose the change that overrides it with least collateral effect.
distractorStrategy: An override that also affects unrelated elements; one that relies on order where the other rule loads later; a blunt instrument that wins but makes future overrides impossible. All options must work; the judgement is about cost.

factStatement: Two stylesheets can produce the same appearance while differing in what they would do to other markup.
familyName: Judging whether two stylesheets are equivalent
measurementObjective: Decide whether two rule sets behave identically for the given markup and for markup they might also match.
distractorStrategy: A pair identical on this markup and different on a sibling; a pair differing only in specificity with no visible effect yet; a genuinely equivalent pair. Reasoning beyond the shown markup is the measurement.

factStatement: A value is a number, string, boolean, array, object, or the two empty values, and each behaves differently.
familyName: Naming the type of a value
measurementObjective: Given values written in code, name each type.
distractorStrategy: An array called an object of no particular kind; a quoted number called a number; the two empty values treated as the same thing. The empty-value pair is the productive case.

factStatement: A variable declared as reassignable can be changed; one declared as constant cannot be reassigned.
familyName: Recognising what a declaration permits
measurementObjective: Say whether a described reassignment is allowed.
distractorStrategy: A constant assumed to make its contents immutable — the real confusion, since a constant array can still be modified; reassignment assumed always allowed; declaration assumed optional.
notes: The constant-array case belongs at D2 and is worth most of this family.

factStatement: Logging displays a value at the moment it runs, and shows the value rather than the expression.
familyName: What a single log produces
measurementObjective: Give what one or two log statements output.
distractorStrategy: The expression shown rather than its value; the variable name printed; the value after a later change rather than at the time of logging.

factStatement: The plus operator adds numbers and joins strings, so the types of its operands decide the result.
familyName: Predicting what plus produces
measurementObjective: Give the result and type of plus applied to mixed operands.
distractorStrategy: A number and a string added numerically; the concatenation given without its quotes hiding the type; an error claimed where the operation is legal. Mixing a number with a numeric string is the essential stem.

factStatement: One equality comparison converts types before comparing and the other does not.
familyName: Deciding whether two values compare equal
measurementObjective: Say whether a comparison holds, for both forms of equality.
distractorStrategy: The two forms treated as identical; the converting form assumed never to match across types; a case where they genuinely agree offered as though they differ. Comparing a number with its string form is the canonical stem.
notes: The highest-value fact in the skill and the source of the most first-year bugs.

factStatement: Zero, the empty string and the empty values are false in a condition; an empty array is not.
familyName: Deciding whether a value passes a condition
measurementObjective: Say whether a condition holds when the value tested is not a boolean.
distractorStrategy: An empty array assumed false — the case that separates this from other languages; zero assumed true; the string "0" assumed false. Each is a defensible guess.

factStatement: Array positions start at zero, the length is one more than the last index, and the contents can be changed in place.
familyName: Reading and changing array contents
measurementObjective: Give the contents or length of an array after described operations.
distractorStrategy: One-based indexing; length confused with the last index; an out-of-range read assumed to fail rather than give an empty value. The last differs from Python and is worth measuring.

factStatement: A function receives arguments and gives back a value; without a return it gives back the empty value.
familyName: What a call evaluates to
measurementObjective: Give what a call produces, including when the function has no return.
distractorStrategy: A logged value assumed to be returned; the empty value reported as zero or as an error; code after the return assumed to run.
notes: Overlaps FUNCTIONS_BASICS by design; different skill, so a separate reassessment group by rule.

factStatement: An object holds values under names, read either by dot or by bracket, and a missing name gives the empty value.
familyName: Reading a value out of an object
measurementObjective: Give the value a described access produces, including for a name that is absent.
distractorStrategy: A missing property assumed to fail rather than give the empty value; bracket access with an unquoted name assumed to work; a nested access assumed safe when the outer value is absent.

factStatement: Assigning an array or object to another name shares it; changing one changes the other.
familyName: Reasoning about two names for one value
measurementObjective: Give the contents of both names after one is modified.
distractorStrategy: The second name assumed to be an independent copy; numbers assumed to share the same way; the original assumed frozen because it was declared constant. All three are held simultaneously by beginners.
notes: The single most consequential JS fact after equality.

factStatement: A fragment combining values, a condition and a loop produces one determinate output.
familyName: Tracing a short fragment to its output
measurementObjective: Give the logged output of a fragment using assignment, a condition and a loop.
distractorStrategy: The result of one extra or one fewer iteration; the value before the final update; the answer from the other branch. Each distractor reachable by one identifiable slip.

factStatement: A fragment can fail to run, fail while running, or run and be wrong, and each has different evidence.
familyName: Diagnosing how a fragment failed
measurementObjective: Given a fragment and what happened, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A logic fault reported as a crash; reading a property of an absent value reported as a silent empty result (it fails); a value that is quietly wrong reported as an error.

factStatement: Automatic type conversion makes some comparisons and sums behave unexpectedly.
familyName: Diagnosing a fault caused by conversion
measurementObjective: Given code producing a surprising result, identify where conversion caused it.
distractorStrategy: The comparison blamed where the concatenation is at fault; a type error claimed where conversion succeeded quietly; the input blamed rather than the operator. D5 uses a total that is a string because one input never converted.
notes: Same fact family as equality; the measurement is diagnosis rather than prediction.

factStatement: Empty arrays, absent properties and the two empty values are where working code stops working.
familyName: Behaviour on empty or absent values
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does when its input is empty or a property is absent.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary-input answer; a crash where the result is quietly wrong; a quiet result where it genuinely crashes. Summing an empty array against averaging one is the sharpest pair.

factStatement: Two fragments can agree on ordinary values and differ on empty, absent or mixed-type ones.
familyName: Judging whether two fragments always agree
measurementObjective: Decide whether two fragments behave identically, and name an input that separates them.
distractorStrategy: A pair differing only on an empty array; one differing only between the two equality forms; a genuinely equivalent pair. All must look interchangeable.

factStatement: The browser turns the markup into a tree of objects that scripts can read and change while the page is open.
familyName: Recognising what the DOM is
measurementObjective: Identify what the DOM is and how it relates to the delivered file.
distractorStrategy: The DOM described as the source file; as a browser feature you enable; as something only frameworks use. The source-file conflation blocks everything else in the skill.

factStatement: Looking for an element gives you that element, a collection, or nothing at all.
familyName: Recognising what a lookup returns
measurementObjective: Say whether a described lookup yields one element, several, or nothing.
distractorStrategy: A single-element lookup assumed to return a collection and vice versa; a failed lookup assumed to throw rather than give nothing. The nothing case causes the commonest DOM crash.

factStatement: Code attached to an event runs when the event happens, not when it is attached.
familyName: Recognising when handler code runs
measurementObjective: Say whether attached code has run yet, at a described point.
distractorStrategy: The handler assumed to run at the moment it is attached — the mistake that produces a call where a reference was wanted; assumed to run once and then detach; assumed to run only after a reload.

factStatement: An element lookup matches the same way a stylesheet selector does.
familyName: Deciding which element a lookup finds
measurementObjective: Given markup and a lookup, say which element or how many are found.
distractorStrategy: A single-result lookup assumed to find the last match rather than the first; a class lookup assumed to find one; a descendant lookup read as requiring a direct child. Show markup in the stem.
notes: Depends on HT_FAM11 and CS_FAM04; the same selector reasoning applied to a different purpose.

factStatement: Reading an element's text gives the words; reading its markup gives the tags as well.
familyName: What reading an element gives you
measurementObjective: Given markup, say what a described read produces.
distractorStrategy: Text read as including the tags; markup read as excluding them; nested element text omitted. Nested markup is required or the two reads look identical.

factStatement: Changing the DOM changes what is displayed now, and does not change the file on the server.
familyName: Reasoning about what a DOM change affects
measurementObjective: Say what a described change affects, and what happens to it on reload.
distractorStrategy: The change assumed to persist across a reload; assumed to edit the source file; assumed visible to other users. This is the belief that makes students think they have saved data.
notes: Builds directly on BR_FAM05.

factStatement: A script can change an element's classes or its inline style, and the cascade then decides the appearance.
familyName: Predicting appearance after a script changes styling
measurementObjective: Given a stylesheet and a script change, say how the element ends up looking.
distractorStrategy: An added class assumed to win over a more specific existing rule; an inline change assumed to lose; a removed class assumed to remove inherited styling too.
notes: Requires CS_FAM06. Do not schedule before cascade has been measured.

factStatement: A handler is told which element the event happened on, and can read or change that element.
familyName: Identifying which element a handler acts on
measurementObjective: Given several similar elements and one handler, say which element is affected by a click.
distractorStrategy: The first matching element affected regardless of which was clicked — the classic bug from attaching to one element instead of each; all matching elements affected; the parent affected.

factStatement: A script running before an element exists cannot find it.
familyName: Reasoning about script position and element availability
measurementObjective: Given a script placed before or after the markup it uses, say whether the lookup succeeds.
distractorStrategy: The script assumed to wait for the page; the failure attributed to a wrong selector; the position assumed irrelevant. This is the single commonest "why is it null" cause.
notes: Show the script tag position in the stem markup.

factStatement: A collection of elements must be iterated; setting a property on the collection itself does nothing.
familyName: Reasoning about acting on many elements
measurementObjective: Say what happens when a change is applied to a collection rather than to its members.
distractorStrategy: The change assumed to apply to all members; assumed to apply to the first; assumed to throw. Silently doing nothing is the real behaviour and the hardest to debug.

factStatement: A value read from a form control is a string, whatever the control looks like.
familyName: Reasoning about the type of a read input
measurementObjective: Predict the result of arithmetic or comparison on a value read from a control.
distractorStrategy: A numeric input assumed to give a number; two values assumed to sum rather than join; an empty control assumed to give the empty value rather than an empty string.
notes: Same shape as PGF_FAM08 and PY_FAM08; different skill and different source, so measured again here.

factStatement: From an element you can reach its parent, children and siblings.
familyName: Reaching a related element
measurementObjective: Given markup and a starting element, identify which element a described traversal reaches.
distractorStrategy: A grandparent reached where a parent was asked; text content counted as an element child; a sibling in a different parent. Requires HT_FAM11.

factStatement: A lookup that finds nothing has a specific cause: the wrong selector, the wrong time, or the element genuinely absent.
familyName: Diagnosing why a lookup found nothing
measurementObjective: Given markup, a script and a failure, identify the cause.
distractorStrategy: A selector cause where the timing is at fault and the reverse; the element blamed where the selector is missing its class prefix; a browser cause proposed. D5 gives a case where two causes are plausible and one detail decides.
notes: The most useful family in the skill: every beginner hits this within a week.

factStatement: A handler that never runs was attached to the wrong element, at the wrong time, or called instead of referenced.
familyName: Diagnosing a handler that never runs
measurementObjective: Given code where nothing happens on click, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: The handler called at attach time rather than referenced — the fault that makes it run once immediately and never again; attached before the element exists; attached to a collection. All three produce "nothing happens" and are separable only by reading.
notes: The distractors are all real causes of the same symptom, which is what makes this D5.

factStatement: Replacing an element's markup, changing its text, and toggling a class have different costs and side effects.
familyName: Choosing how to update the page
measurementObjective: Given a required change, choose the approach with the fewest side effects.
distractorStrategy: Replacing markup where a class toggle suffices, which discards attached handlers; changing text where markup was needed; rebuilding the whole list to change one item. All options must work visually; the judgement is about what breaks.
notes: Losing handlers by replacing markup is the transfer insight worth most here.

factStatement: The browser requests files from a server and turns them into what you see.
familyName: Recognising the browser's job
measurementObjective: Identify which parts of getting a page onto the screen the browser performs.
distractorStrategy: The browser described as storing the whole web; as running the server; as the internet itself. The last is a real belief and worth measuring once.

factStatement: An address has distinguishable parts — scheme, host and path — each with a different job.
familyName: Identifying the parts of an address
measurementObjective: Given an address, name the host or the path.
distractorStrategy: The path named as the host; the scheme included in the host; a subdomain read as a path segment.

factStatement: Developer tools show the page as it currently is, which may differ from the file on disk.
familyName: Knowing what developer tools reveal
measurementObjective: Identify which question developer tools can answer.
distractorStrategy: Developer tools assumed to edit the source file; assumed to show the server's code; assumed to be a separate program from the browser. The first matters: students expect their edits to persist.

factStatement: A page arrives as a document that then requests the other files it references.
familyName: Ordering what happens when a page loads
measurementObjective: Put the stages of loading a page in order.
distractorStrategy: All files assumed to arrive together; images assumed to arrive before the document that names them; the page assumed to render only when everything has arrived.

factStatement: What is on screen is the current state of the page, which scripts may have changed since it arrived.
familyName: Distinguishing the delivered file from the live page
measurementObjective: Say whether a described difference means the file changed or the page was modified after loading.
distractorStrategy: The source assumed to always match the screen; a script-made change assumed to be in the file; the file assumed to update when the page does.
notes: Prepares the ground for JS_DOM without requiring it.

factStatement: The browser may reuse a stored copy of a file rather than requesting it again.
familyName: Reasoning about what a cached copy causes
measurementObjective: Say what a user sees after a file changes on the server but a copy is cached.
distractorStrategy: Every request assumed to reach the server; caching assumed to affect the whole page rather than individual files; a hard refresh assumed to be the only way anything updates.

factStatement: A cookie is small data the browser stores and sends back with later requests to the same site.
familyName: Reasoning about what a cookie does
measurementObjective: Say what happens to stored site data across page loads and across sites.
distractorStrategy: Cookies assumed shared between unrelated sites; assumed stored on the server; assumed to survive being cleared. The cross-site case is the one that matters for privacy reasoning.

factStatement: The browser restricts what a page from one site may do with content from another.
familyName: Reasoning about cross-site restrictions
measurementObjective: Say whether a described cross-site action is permitted and why.
distractorStrategy: Any request to another site assumed blocked; all assumed permitted; the restriction attributed to the server rather than the browser. Displaying an image versus reading a response is the discriminating pair.
notes: Conceptual. No header names at Foundation.

factStatement: Data the browser stores for a site is visible only to that site, in that browser, on that device.
familyName: Reasoning about where stored data is visible
measurementObjective: Say whether stored data is available in another browser, on another device, or to another site.
distractorStrategy: Stored data assumed to follow the user across devices; assumed shared with the server automatically; assumed visible to any site. Students routinely conflate local storage with an account.

factStatement: Every file the page requested can be inspected, with its address and whether it arrived.
familyName: Answering a question from a request list
measurementObjective: Given a list of requests in the stem, say which file failed or was served from cache.
distractorStrategy: A successful request read as failed; a cached response read as a fresh one; a missing file assumed to be a code fault. The list must decide the answer.
notes: Show a small request table in the stem.

conceptName: Why is my change not showing
factStatement: A change that is in the file and not on the screen was not saved, not requested again, or served from a stored copy.
familyName: Diagnosing a change that is not visible
measurementObjective: Given the symptom, identify why the browser is not showing the new version.
distractorStrategy: The code blamed where the cause is caching; caching blamed where the file was never saved; the wrong file edited. All three happen weekly to a first-year and the evidence must separate them.

conceptName: What the browser can be trusted with
factStatement: Anything the browser holds or checks can be changed by the person using it.
familyName: Judging what may be relied on in the browser
measurementObjective: Decide whether a described check is sufficient on its own.
distractorStrategy: A browser-side check treated as enforcement; hiding a control treated as preventing the action; stored data treated as tamper-proof. This is the foundation of every later security idea.

conceptName: Why is my change not showing
factStatement: A page missing part of itself usually has one failed request, and which part is missing says which one.
familyName: Identifying which request failed from what is missing
measurementObjective: Given a page rendering without its styling or an image, identify the failed request and likely cause.
distractorStrategy: A cause that would break the whole page rather than one part; a path error where the file is genuinely absent; a cache cause where nothing was ever cached. D5 gives two failures with one visible symptom.

factStatement: Private browsing stops the browser keeping local records; it does not hide activity from the network or the site.
familyName: Reasoning about what private browsing does not do
measurementObjective: Given a described concern, decide whether private browsing addresses it.
distractorStrategy: Private mode assumed to hide traffic from a network operator; assumed to prevent a site identifying a returning user; assumed to make requests anonymous. Every option must be a real belief.
notes: Genuine transfer: the student must reason from what is stored where, not recall a feature list.

factStatement: How long a file may be reused is a choice that trades speed against showing stale content.
familyName: Choosing how long content may be reused
measurementObjective: Given content that changes at a stated rate, choose a caching approach and say what it costs.
distractorStrategy: Long reuse for content that changes constantly; no reuse for content that never changes; a choice that ignores the stated change rate. The rate must decide the answer.

factStatement: A client sends a request and the server sends back one response; the server does not start the exchange.
familyName: Recognising the shape of an exchange
measurementObjective: Identify which side sends what, and in which order.
distractorStrategy: The server described as initiating; the exchange described as continuous; the response described as optional. Ties to HCW_FAM12 but measured as the protocol rather than the roles.

factStatement: The method states what the client intends — to fetch something or to change something.
familyName: Recognising what a method means
measurementObjective: Given a method, say whether it is asking for data or asking for a change.
distractorStrategy: A fetch method described as changing data; a change method described as read-only; the method assumed to be decided by the server. Keep to the two or three methods a first-year meets.

factStatement: A status belongs to a class — success, client fault, server fault — and the class says who has the problem.
familyName: Recognising what a status class means
measurementObjective: Given a status, say whether the request succeeded and which side was at fault.
distractorStrategy: A client fault read as a server fault; a redirect read as a failure; any non-success read as a server problem. Classes, not individual numbers — the number is only evidence.
notes: Deliberately about classes so the family cannot degrade into memorising a table.

factStatement: A request carries a method, an address, headers and sometimes a body; a response carries a status, headers and usually a body.
familyName: Identifying the parts of a message
measurementObjective: Given a request or response shown in the stem, identify a named part.
distractorStrategy: A header read as body content; the address read as a header; the status read as part of the body. Show a real message shape.

factStatement: The server does not remember previous requests unless something in the new request tells it who is asking.
familyName: Reasoning about what the server remembers
measurementObjective: Say what the server knows about a client on a second request.
distractorStrategy: The server assumed to remember automatically; the connection assumed to persist as a session; the browser assumed to be identified by address alone.
notes: Explains why the cookie in BR_FAM07 has to exist.

factStatement: Using a fetch method for something that changes data is wrong, because fetches may be repeated or cached.
familyName: Choosing the method an action needs
measurementObjective: Given an action, choose the appropriate method and say what goes wrong otherwise.
distractorStrategy: A fetch used for a change, with the consequence stated wrongly; a change method used for a read; a choice justified by convenience rather than by effect. The consequence must be the discriminator.

factStatement: The status class tells you whether to look at the request or at the server.
familyName: Deciding which side to investigate
measurementObjective: Given a status and a symptom, say where the fault is and what to check.
distractorStrategy: A client fault investigated on the server; a server fault attributed to a bad address; a success status with an empty body read as a failure. The last is a real and confusing case.

factStatement: The path names what is being asked for; the query supplies extra parameters.
familyName: Reasoning about path against query
measurementObjective: Given a requirement, choose the address that expresses it correctly.
distractorStrategy: A filter placed in the path where it is a parameter; an identifier placed in the query where it names the resource; parameters concatenated without separators. Builds on BR_FAM02.

factStatement: Headers describe the message — what it contains, who is asking — rather than being the content.
familyName: Reasoning about what a header conveys
measurementObjective: Say what a described header tells the other side.
distractorStrategy: A header read as body content; a content-type header assumed to convert the body; a header assumed to be enforced by the protocol. No header-name recall — the stem states the header's purpose.

factStatement: A secure connection protects the message in transit; it says nothing about what the server does with it.
familyName: Reasoning about what a secure connection guarantees
measurementObjective: Given a concern, decide whether a secure connection addresses it.
distractorStrategy: Encryption assumed to make the site trustworthy; assumed to hide which site was visited; assumed to protect data once stored. All three are widely believed.

factStatement: A server knows who is asking only from what the request carries.
familyName: Reasoning about how a server recognises a client
measurementObjective: Say what happens to a described action when the identifying data is missing.
distractorStrategy: Identity assumed to persist in the connection; assumed inferable from the address; assumed unnecessary because the user is logged in in another tab.

factStatement: A response may be stored and reused, which is why a repeated request can return old data.
familyName: Reasoning about a reused response
measurementObjective: Say whether a repeated request reaches the server, and what the client receives.
distractorStrategy: Every request assumed to reach the server; reuse assumed to apply to change requests too; stale data blamed on the server. Complements BR_FAM06 from the protocol side.

factStatement: The status, the body and whether the request arrived at all together locate the fault.
familyName: Locating the fault in a failed exchange
measurementObjective: Given the evidence from a failed request, identify the cause.
distractorStrategy: A cause that would produce a different status; a server cause where the request never left; a wrong-address cause where the address was right and the resource absent. D5 gives a request that succeeded with a body describing a failure.
notes: A success status carrying an error body is the most instructive case and the hardest.

factStatement: Everything in a request comes from the client and can be changed by whoever sends it.
familyName: Judging what a server may rely on
measurementObjective: Decide whether a described server-side assumption about the request is safe.
distractorStrategy: A value from the request trusted because the page set it; a hidden field trusted; a header trusted as proof of identity. Extends BR_FAM12 to the server side, which is the transfer.

factStatement: How an action is expressed — method, address, what is returned — is a design choice with consequences.
familyName: Choosing how to express an action
measurementObjective: Given a required action, choose the method, address and response shape and justify it.
distractorStrategy: A design that works but is unsafe to repeat; one that returns nothing useful to the caller; one that puts state-changing intent in a fetch. All must be functional; the reasoning is about consequence.
notes: No REST vocabulary at Foundation; the judgement is about repeatability and clarity.

factStatement: In C a variable is declared with a type before use, and that type does not change.
familyName: Recognising a valid declaration
measurementObjective: Identify which declarations are well formed and what type each name has.
distractorStrategy: A declaration without a type — valid in Python and not here; a type changed by a later assignment; two names declared with one type where the syntax does not allow it.
notes: Measured because it is exactly where C differs from the language taught first.

factStatement: Each type holds a limited range of values, and a whole-number type cannot hold a fraction.
familyName: Recognising what a type can hold
measurementObjective: Say whether a given value fits the declared type.
distractorStrategy: A fractional value assumed to be stored in a whole-number type; a character type assumed to hold a word; a whole-number type assumed unbounded.

factStatement: Printing a value requires a specifier that matches its type.
familyName: Matching a value to its output specifier
measurementObjective: Given a value and a specifier, say what is printed or that they do not match.
distractorStrategy: A whole-number specifier used for a fraction; a mismatch assumed to be corrected automatically; a mismatch assumed to be refused at compile time when it is not. The third is the important one.
notes: Foundation-critical: a mismatch produces nonsense rather than an error, which beginners cannot explain.

factStatement: A declared variable holds an unpredictable value until something is assigned to it.
familyName: Reasoning about an unassigned variable
measurementObjective: Say what a program does when it reads a variable before assigning to it.
distractorStrategy: An unassigned variable assumed to be zero — the belief that makes accumulator bugs invisible; assumed to cause a compile failure; assumed to be the same value every run.

factStatement: Dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number, discarding any remainder.
familyName: Predicting the result of whole-number division
measurementObjective: Give the result of a division where both operands are whole numbers.
distractorStrategy: The fractional result; the result rounded rather than truncated; the remainder. Rounding versus truncation is the discriminator and requires a value like 7/2.
notes: The commonest silent C bug for a student arriving from Python.

factStatement: Mixing a whole number with a fractional one converts before the operation, which changes the result.
familyName: Predicting the result of mixed-type arithmetic
measurementObjective: Give the result and type of an expression mixing whole and fractional values.
distractorStrategy: The whole-number result where conversion makes it fractional; conversion assumed to happen before an earlier whole-number division that already truncated; the result assumed to take the declared type of the target.
notes: Truncation before conversion is the D4 case and the one that matters.

factStatement: Reading a value requires saying where to put it as well as what type to expect.
familyName: Reasoning about a read that goes wrong
measurementObjective: Say what happens when a read is given a mismatched type or no destination.
distractorStrategy: A mismatch assumed to convert; a missing destination marker assumed harmless; the read assumed to fail loudly rather than leave the variable untouched.
notes: Conceptual: the stem states what the read is trying to do.

factStatement: An array has a size fixed at declaration, and its valid positions run from zero to one less than that size.
familyName: Reasoning about valid array positions
measurementObjective: Given a declared size, say which positions are valid.
distractorStrategy: The size used as the last valid position; positions counted from one; the array assumed to grow. The size-as-index error is the direct cause of the next family.

factStatement: Reading or writing outside an array is not detected; the program continues with meaningless data.
familyName: Reasoning about access past the end
measurementObjective: Say what a program does when it accesses beyond an array.
distractorStrategy: An error message assumed; the value assumed to be zero; a crash assumed to be guaranteed. The truth — that it may appear to work — is the whole measurement, and it is what separates C from Python.
notes: The most important safety fact in the skill.

factStatement: Text is stored as characters ending with a terminator, so it needs one more position than it has letters.
familyName: Reasoning about the space text needs
measurementObjective: Say how many positions are needed to store given text, and what happens if there is one too few.
distractorStrategy: The terminator forgotten so the count is one short; the terminator counted twice; the array assumed to size itself. Off-by-one here produces exactly the D4 case.

factStatement: The declared types of the variables change what a sequence of statements produces.
familyName: Tracing a fragment where the types matter
measurementObjective: Give the printed output of a fragment whose result depends on its declared types.
distractorStrategy: The answer that would be right with fractional types throughout; the answer with the truncation applied at the wrong step; an intermediate value. The declaration must decide the answer.

factStatement: A C program can compile, run, and be wrong, and the absence of an error message says nothing.
familyName: Diagnosing a fault the compiler did not catch
measurementObjective: Given a program that runs and gives a wrong result, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A compile-time complaint offered where the fault is at run time; an uninitialised variable blamed where truncation is the cause; the input blamed. Distinguishing the two silent causes is the measurement.

factStatement: A truncation early in a calculation cannot be recovered later, however the result is stored.
familyName: Diagnosing a result lost to truncation
measurementObjective: Given an average or proportion that comes out wrong, identify where precision was lost and what would fix it.
distractorStrategy: Storing the result in a fractional type offered as the fix, which does not help; the output specifier blamed; the operands blamed. Only converting BEFORE the division works, and that must be the sole correct option.
notes: The canonical C stem: an average of whole numbers that comes out whole.

factStatement: Zero, negative and very large values expose the limits of a declared type.
familyName: Behaviour at the limits of a type
measurementObjective: Say what a fragment does for zero, negative or out-of-range input.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary-input answer; an error assumed where the value silently wraps or truncates; a wrap assumed where the value is in range. Negative whole-number division is the sharpest case.

factStatement: The same algorithm written in C and in a dynamically typed language differs in specific, predictable ways.
familyName: Predicting where the same code behaves differently
measurementObjective: Given the same algorithm in both, identify the input on which they disagree and why.
distractorStrategy: A difference claimed where both agree; the difference attributed to speed rather than to types; an out-of-range access claimed to fail in both. Genuine transfer: neither language alone contains the answer.
notes: Worth the D5 weight — it is the point of teaching C alongside Python at all.

factStatement: A control structure governs one statement, or a braced block of them; indentation has no effect.
familyName: Identifying which statements a structure governs
measurementObjective: Given a fragment, say which statements are inside the structure.
distractorStrategy: Indentation trusted over braces — the essential C trap and unavailable in Python; a semicolon after the condition treated as harmless; braces assumed compulsory. Show misleading indentation deliberately.
notes: Misleading indentation is the whole point of this family and must appear in every variant.

factStatement: A condition is true when its value is not zero, so any number can be used as a condition.
familyName: Recognising what counts as true
measurementObjective: Say whether a given numeric condition is satisfied.
distractorStrategy: Only one specific value assumed true; a negative number assumed false; a non-comparison expression assumed invalid as a condition.

factStatement: One loop form tests before the body and another tests after, so one may run zero times and the other at least once.
familyName: Recognising which loop form runs at least once
measurementObjective: Say which form guarantees one execution of the body.
distractorStrategy: Both forms assumed to test first; both assumed to run at least once; the counted form assumed to be the one that always runs. This distinction does not exist in the first language taught.

factStatement: Assignment inside a condition stores a value and then tests it, so it is almost never what was meant.
familyName: Reasoning about a single-equals condition
measurementObjective: Say what a condition containing an assignment evaluates to and what it changes.
distractorStrategy: The assignment read as a comparison; the condition assumed to fail to compile; the variable assumed unchanged. All three miss half of what happens, and the correct answer must state both effects.
notes: The classic C trap. Not available in Python, so it must be measured here.

factStatement: An else belongs to the nearest unmatched if, whatever the indentation suggests.
familyName: Deciding which if an else belongs to
measurementObjective: Given nested conditionals without braces, say which branch runs.
distractorStrategy: The else bound as the indentation suggests; the else assumed to apply to the outer if; both branches assumed to run. Indentation must contradict the real binding.

factStatement: A counted loop states its start, its continuing condition and its step, and the three together decide how many times it runs.
familyName: How many times a counted loop runs
measurementObjective: Give the number of executions for stated start, condition and step.
distractorStrategy: One too many from reading the condition as inclusive; the difference between the bounds where the step is not one; the count when the step moves away from the bound so it never ends.

factStatement: The loop variable keeps the value that ended the loop, which is past the last one used.
familyName: What the counter holds afterwards
measurementObjective: Give the counter value after the loop finishes.
distractorStrategy: The last value used in the body; the starting value; the bound minus one. Off by exactly one, which is the point.

factStatement: An accumulator must be given a starting value before the loop, because an unassigned variable holds anything.
familyName: Reasoning about a total built in a loop
measurementObjective: Say what a loop total produces, given where its accumulator is initialised.
distractorStrategy: An unassigned accumulator assumed to start at zero — far more consequential in C than in Python; initialisation inside the loop assumed harmless; the total assumed correct because the program ran.
notes: Depends on CC_FAM04.

conceptName: Leaving a loop or a case
factStatement: A break leaves the innermost loop or case block, not all of them.
familyName: Reasoning about what a break leaves
measurementObjective: Given nested structures, say where execution continues after a break.
distractorStrategy: The break assumed to leave both loops; assumed to leave the function; assumed to skip one iteration. Nested loops are required.

factStatement: Without a break, execution continues into the following case.
familyName: Reasoning about a missing break
measurementObjective: Give the output of a multi-way selection with a missing break.
distractorStrategy: Only the matching case assumed to run; all cases assumed to run; the default assumed to run whenever anything matched. Deliberate fall-through must appear so it is not simply an error.
notes: No Python equivalent, which is why it belongs here.

factStatement: An inner loop completes for every iteration of the outer one, and its variables reset if declared inside.
familyName: Tracing nested loops in C
measurementObjective: Give the total inner executions or the output of a nested pair.
distractorStrategy: The bounds added rather than multiplied; the inner counter assumed to carry over between outer iterations; a dependent inner bound treated as fixed. The carry-over case is the C-specific one.

factStatement: A return ends the function immediately, including from inside a loop.
familyName: Reasoning about a return inside a loop
measurementObjective: Say what a function returns when its return sits inside a loop.
distractorStrategy: The loop assumed to finish first; the return assumed to act like a break; the last value assumed returned rather than the first. Returning on the first iteration is the classic fault.

factStatement: A stray semicolon, a missing brace or a missing break compiles and changes what the program does.
familyName: Diagnosing a control-flow fault that compiled
measurementObjective: Given a program that runs and behaves wrongly, identify the control-flow fault.
distractorStrategy: A compile error offered where the code is valid; the condition blamed where a semicolon terminated the loop body; the loop bound blamed where a brace is missing. Each fault must produce a distinguishable symptom.
notes: A semicolon immediately after a loop header is the sharpest D5 stem: an empty body and a symptom far away.

factStatement: Loops that run zero times, or exactly once, expose faults that ordinary input hides.
familyName: Tracing a C loop at its boundary
measurementObjective: Say what a loop produces when its bound makes it run zero or one times.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary answer; the test-after form assumed to run zero times; an uninitialised accumulator printed as zero. Combining a zero-iteration loop with an uninitialised total is the strongest D5 stem.

factStatement: The same behaviour can be written with different control structures, and some rewrites change the boundary cases.
familyName: Judging whether two control structures behave the same
measurementObjective: Decide whether two fragments behave identically, and name the input that separates them.
distractorStrategy: A test-before rewritten as a test-after, which differs only on zero iterations; a chain rewritten as separate conditionals, which differs when two conditions hold; a genuinely equivalent pair.
notes: The zero-iteration case is what makes the first pair inequivalent, and it is the insight worth transferring.

factStatement: An array holds items in order at numbered positions starting from zero.
familyName: Reading a value at a position
measurementObjective: Given an array, name the value at a stated position or the position of a value.
distractorStrategy: One-based counting; the last position given as the length; a negative position assumed invalid where the language allows it. Show the array with its values in the stem.

factStatement: The length is the number of items; the last position is one less than that.
familyName: Distinguishing length from last position
measurementObjective: Given an array, give its length and its last valid position.
distractorStrategy: The two treated as the same number; length counted from zero; an empty array assumed to have length one. Every off-by-one bug later traces to this.

conceptName: What you can do to an array
factStatement: Reading, replacing, inserting, removing and searching are distinct operations with different effects.
familyName: Recognising what an operation does
measurementObjective: Given a described change, name the operation and say whether the length changes.
distractorStrategy: Replacing confused with inserting — the length is the discriminator; removing assumed to leave a gap; searching assumed to change the array.

conceptName: What you can do to an array
factStatement: Inserting or removing in the middle moves every item after that position.
familyName: What happens to positions after an insertion
measurementObjective: Give the array contents and the new position of a named item after an insertion or removal.
distractorStrategy: Items assumed to stay at their old positions; the shift applied in the wrong direction; the item at the insertion point assumed overwritten. The overwriting case is the insert/replace confusion again, now traced.

factStatement: A traversal visits each item once, and what it does at each item decides the result.
familyName: What a traversal produces
measurementObjective: Give the result of a described traversal — a total, a count, a maximum — over stated data.
distractorStrategy: The total where a count was asked; a maximum computed from a wrong starting value; the first or last item missed. Show the data so the answer is checkable.

factStatement: Finding an item in unsorted data means checking items one by one, and the worst case checks all of them.
familyName: How much work an unsorted search does
measurementObjective: Give the number of comparisons a search makes for a stated target and data.
distractorStrategy: The best case given where the worst was asked; the count when the item is absent given as the length minus one; the position given instead of the comparison count. Ask about an absent item at D4.

factStatement: In sorted data a comparison can rule out half the remaining items, so far fewer checks are needed.
familyName: Reasoning about halving a sorted range
measurementObjective: Say which items remain in consideration after a stated comparison, or how many checks are needed.
distractorStrategy: Half discarded from the wrong side; the halving applied to unsorted data — the essential precondition; the count given as half the length rather than as repeated halving.
notes: The precondition matters more than the arithmetic and should be tested directly at D4.

factStatement: A simple sort makes repeated passes, and after each pass more of the data is in its final place.
familyName: The state of the data after one pass
